_note: SEED DATA — not live. Curated symptom→specialty navigation notes for RAG triage. These map common complaints to the RIGHT TYPE of doctor. They are NOT diagnoses and never name a disease or treatment — only which specialty a patient should consider seeing. Specialties must match seed_facilities.json.

notes.text: Chest pain or chest tightness, pressure or heaviness in the chest, palpitations or a racing/irregular heartbeat, breathlessness on exertion, fainting spells, or swelling of the ankles are typically seen by a Cardiology (heart) specialist. Severe or sudden chest pain with sweating or breathlessness is an emergency.
Skin rashes, itching, acne, eczema, persistent dry or flaky skin, changes in a mole, hair loss, nail problems, or fungal infections are handled by a Dermatology (skin) specialist.

Ear pain, hearing difficulty, ringing in the ears, blocked or runny nose, sinus pressure, sore throat that will not settle, hoarseness, tonsil problems, or dizziness/vertigo are seen by an ENT (ear, nose and throat) specialist.

Health concerns for a baby, infant, child or teenager — fever in a child, childhood vaccinations, feeding or growth concerns, or a sick young child — are seen by a Pediatrics (children's health) specialist.

Long-standing adult conditions such as diabetes, high blood pressure, thyroid problems, persistent fatigue, unexplained weight change, or managing several chronic illnesses together are handled by an Internal Medicine physician.

Common everyday complaints — mild fever, cough and cold, general aches, minor infections, a first check-up, or when you are unsure which specialist you need — start with a General Practice (GP / family doctor) consultation, who can refer you onward.
Headache, body aches, tiredness, mild stomach upset, or a general feeling of being unwell with no clear single cause are usually seen first by a General Practice doctor.
Stomach pain, acid reflux or heartburn, ongoing digestive problems, or abnormal blood-sugar and cholesterol results in an adult are commonly reviewed by an Internal Medicine physician.
